# Related work

RI can be formulated as a selective observation problem and studied within the
framework of missing-data theory. As such it also must handle statistical questions
like identification, sample selection, as well as estimation and evaluation under bias.
The review of @ehrhardt2021rejectReview revealed many structural problems in
existing RI-methods. Among these structural issues, one problem stands out in particular:
just as in @HandHanley1993CanRIWork, the conclusion is
that for RI to perform (distinctly) better than using only the accepts, one needs additional
identifying assumptions or supplementary information beyond the observed accepted outcomes
and applicant covariates. Furthermore, in a
spirit close to @ehrhardt2021rejectReview, I believe that being explicit about
the assumptions both on the data generating process studied, and the methodology
help to rigorously assess the feasibility, potential, limitations and possible
application fields of an RI approach, besides helping to formulate meaningful experimental
settings.

Because the central concern of this thesis is not merely whether a particular RI
procedure performs well, but under which conditions information about rejected
applicants can be obtained from the available data, the literature is reviewed
along four dimensions:

- What information from the rejects does the RI-method exploit, and under what
  assumptions does this information identify the target of interest?
- Are the assumptions concerning the data-generating process, observation mechanism,
  and methodology explicitly stated and theoretically/heuristically justified?
- How do authors evaluate the validity, effectiveness, robustness, and practical
  applicability of their proposed approach, and what limitations do they identify?
- To what extent does the methodology account for the temporal and feedback structure
  induced by repeated acceptance decisions?

All of this information is summarized in table
\ref{tbl-lit-review}.
There these dimensions of the literature analysis have been divided in several dimensions.
For each paper, I document the specific **RI Approach** and the **Key Identifying Assumptions**
required for the method to perform (meaningfully) in practice. Thereby I try to keep implicit
assumptions to a minimum and to formulate them in such way that make the proposed approach
as sensible as possible. I track whether these
assumptions are openly acknowledged and considered (**Assump. Explicit?**), and whether the
authors provide a rigorous **Theoretical or Heuristic Justification** for their model's
viability. These flags as boolean values are sometimes insufficient, as the authors may
for example consider almost all assumptions but a hidden one. The criterion to setting both
of them to true is whether the most important assumptions where made explicit (either by citing
a known methodology, from which its assumptions can be deduced or by stating them specifically)
*and* the narrative of the paper (discussion, experimental design, etc.) is consistent with
the assumptions/justification. Finally, I classify the Result Type (theoretical, empirical,
or simulated), the data basis on which the results were shown (if data was used), summarize
the paper's consensus on whether **RI actually works**, pinpoint the **Main Challenge** limiting
the approach (such as computational scalability or error propagation), and indicate whether the
framework incorporates a **Dynamic Perspective** to account for the self-reinforcing nature
of selection bias across successive lending cycles.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import os
import bibtexparser
#os.chdir("..")
path_lit_tbl_xl = "./data/table_literature_review.xlsx"

lit_review_tbl = pd.read_excel(path_lit_tbl_xl)

boolean_cols = lit_review_tbl.columns[lit_review_tbl.dtypes == bool]

boolean_is_true_str = r"$\checkmark$"
boolan_is_false_str = r''

lit_review_tbl[boolean_cols] = lit_review_tbl[boolean_cols].map(lambda x : boolean_is_true_str if x else boolan_is_false_str)

# Get year information out of the references file
bib_path = "./references.bib"
bib = bibtexparser.parse_file(bib_path)

year_author_idx = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(
  [(
    int(bib.entries_dict[ref].fields_dict["year"].value),
    bib.entries_dict[ref].fields_dict["author"].value.replace("{", '').replace('}', ''),
  )
  for ref in lit_review_tbl["Reference"].values],
  names=("Year", "Author(s)")
)

lit_review_tbl.index = year_author_idx
lit_review_tbl.sort_index(inplace=True)

fun_reflbl_to_ref = lambda ref : f"\\textcite{{{ref}}}" if True else f"@{ref}"#ref
ref_colname = lit_review_tbl.columns[0]

lit_review_tbl[ref_colname] = lit_review_tbl[ref_colname].apply(fun_reflbl_to_ref)
```


```{python}
#| output: asis

widths = [
    0.075, # references
    0.16, # RI Approach
    0.15, # Key identifiying
    0.065, # Ass. explicit
    0.06, #Th heur just
    0.055, # Type result
    0.065, # Eval. pool
    0.08, # Can RI work
    0.115, # main challenge
    0.055, # dynamic persp
]
alignements = ["C" if c in boolean_cols else "p" for c in lit_review_tbl.columns]

total_width_wished = 0.74
sum_widhts = sum(widths)
norm = sum_widhts/total_width_wished
footnote = (
    "The used abbreviations mean: assump. = assumptions, heur. = heuristically, "
    "theo. = theoretical/theoretically, persp. = perspective, emp.=empirical, sim.=simulation, "
    "PD = Probability of Default, EM = Expectation Maximization, AR=Accept/Rejects, GB = Goods/Bads. For the Evaluation "
    r"Pool column: All refer to holdout samples with $\mathbf{A}$ accepts, $\mathbf{R}$ rejects,"
    r" $\mathbf{R}_e$ extrapolated rejects and $\mathbf{AR}_s$ are accepts that were divided into "
    " `simulated' accepts and rejects according to some criterion."
)

lit_review_tbl.columns = [f"\\textbf{{{c}}}" for c in lit_review_tbl.columns]
tex_tbl = (
    lit_review_tbl
    .to_latex(
        escape=False,
        index=False,
        caption="Literature Review",
        label="tbl-lit-review",
        #position="t!",
        longtable=True,
        column_format= "".join(
            [a + f'{{{w / norm}\\linewidth}}' for a, w in zip(alignements, widths)]
        )
    )
)

print(
    r"""
\tiny
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.5}
%\clearpage
    """
)
begin_footnote = (
  "\\midrule\n"
  rf"\multicolumn{{{lit_review_tbl.shape[1]}}}"
  r"{p{0.96\linewidth}}{"
)
footnote_wrapped = (
  begin_footnote +
    r"""
\textit{Note:} """ + footnote +
r"""
}\\
\end{longtable}
"""
)
print(tex_tbl.replace(r'\end{longtable}', footnote_wrapped))
print(r"""
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1}
\normalsize
"""
)
```

Consistent with the findings of @ehrhardt2021rejectReview I see that often the assumptions
are not explicit, which I find to be harmful for the credibility of the proposals and even
to lead to contradictions. For example @XiaEtAl2018RIPesimisticLikelihood fail to identify
that the proposed weighting scheme requires the model's PD to be calibrated to be meaningful.
Thereby they use standard LightGBM, which per se is not ensured to be calibrated. Furthermore, it is
interesting to find cases like @ChenAstebro2010RIBoundCollapseBayesian where even though
MNAR is assumed explicitly, they simulate rejects and accepts pool from the labeled accepts
by choosing cut-offs with a MAR mechanism. Another case worth highlighting is
@ElAnnas2022SemisupervisedAH. They implicitly assume that a Markov chain along the features can be meaningfully
tied to hidden states related to the loan outcomes, which is achieved algorithmically, and
the empirical results seem to support the claim. However, they fail to discuss which role
the order of the features play and also whether a semantic relationship is thereby ensured,
making it questionable to what extent the found success of the approach is just "good luck"
in the made experiment. These observations strengthen my belief in the utility of being explicit
on which assumptions are made when studying the RI problem.

Also, @Anderson2019BayesianNetForRI exemplifies, that being explicit with the assumptions
does not necessarily mean that they are well pondered to make a good analysis of
the proposed approach. See that they do not justify their approach (second column). In their case
it is assumed that causal non-cyclic relationships between features are given, but it is
not argued under which circumstances this should be expected. For example, the marital status
and the assets hold by an applicant are not necessarily acyclic. It could be in some cases
that someone gets married (partly) because of its assets, but then it buys more assets to
provide a better living standard for its spouse. In general, I found that the lack of a
heuristic or theoretical justification for the approach always weakened the credibility of
the approach, which can make it harder to make RI a standard for the industry.
Nonetheless, being explicit on both assumptions and justification is not foolproof.
E.g. @ShenEtAl2020ThreeStageRI vouch for the usage of
Self-Thought-Learning for higher level features representation because it does not require
the accepts and rejects features to belong to the same region, but they also use three-way
decision theory to select rejects for STL that are alike to the accepts in the Mahalanobis
Distance sense. I.e. they choose rejects that could be expected to come from the same features'
distribution as the accepts.

It also stands out that although many papers introduce the RI problem as an open problem
without (really) promising solutions, a fair amount of papers in table
\ref{tbl-lit-review}
conclude that their own method works, at least moderately. This conclusion is however often
hard to believe. On the one hand some papers like @LiEtAl2017SemisupervisedSVM and
@TianEtAl2018RIKernelFreeFuzzySVM evaluate the RI method by using a (partially) extrapolated
sample containing also rejects, which inherently leads to a circular relation.
On the other hand other papers, generate artificial rejects from the accepts by
using some rule to hide to the learner the labels of some of the accepts
[@ChenAstebro2010RIBoundCollapseBayesian; @MaldonadoParedes2010SemiSupSVM; @ribeiro2025balancingperformancerejectinclusion]. 
This is however filtering further the accepts that should already belong to the most
creditworthy part of the population, which is likely not very representative of
a real dataset. Simulation based work also sometimes uses an unrealistic DGP
like @BuckerEtAl2013MNARRI which assumes observability, outcome and features
are i.i.d. across the applicants, which is not likely in a dynamic environment or
@Feelders2000RIMixtureModels who uses a very abstract decision rule. See that the
unrealistic DGP is accompanied by a lack of explicit modeling from the FI's reality
to a mathematical description of the DGP. The rest of the papers base their results on
changes of some classification metric on holdout accepts. This approach is likely too narrow,
as it is hard to generalize those results to an understanding of how an RI based acceptance
policy would perform. One option is using metrics designed specifically for the RI problem,
which seem to be more adequate to evaluate the performance of RI approaches
[@ribeiro2025balancingperformancerejectinclusion; @kozdoi_et_al_BE_BASL]. Another one, that
is hard to implement, is doing A/B testing like @KangEtAl2021GraphBasedSemiRI, which would
be the best possible way to actually prove if the method works.

Now it is also worth taking a look into the most promising proposals, meaning the ones that
can show good results in a sensible experimental setting, do not base on unplausible
assumptions and have a convincing evaluation method given the approach. These are for me
only four: Bayesian Evaluation [@kozdoi_et_al_BE_BASL], cost sensitive S3VM with JDA
[@ShengEtAl2024RICostSenstiveJointDistAdap] and the seminal semi-supervised SVM for credit
scoring [@MaldonadoParedes2010SemiSupSVM].^[
  See that this model is not the most common benchmark with the literature tending to
  prefer the kernel based SVM of @LiEtAl2017SemisupervisedSVM. I still prefer this work
  as it remains a base on which the literature develops new methods and is a work that
  fulfills the aforementioned conditions.
]
Besides Bayesian Evaluation, all of these methods base on further assumptions, reinforcing
the findings of @ehrhardt2021rejectReview and @HandHanley1993CanRIWork on the necessity
of further identifying assumptions. See that among the complete literature review no paper
has used the inherent dynamic nature of the RI problem in credit scoring. I believe this
aspect can help to develop a new sensible assumption while developing RI methods.

In conclusion the literature review has found three fundamental issues, which seem to be
weakening at least an important part the research. First is not considering which assumptions
are needed for the approach to work and the ground question on why is it worth a shot trying
out the proposed methodology. To address this I carefully explain my assumptions on the DGP
and make transparent how I have implemented them, including a narrative on why this simulation
is a valid way to study the RI problem by tying it to an FI's point of view
(Sec. @sec-theor-bg-and-problem-setting and @sec-sim-framework). Second, it seems like it
is indispensable to use further assumptions than the typical ones made in credit scoring
or "vanilla" classification problems. As an answer I propose the hypothesis of a
self-reinforcing acceptance-bias as a plausible assumption that can be used to help identify
new models through *surprise* (Sec. @sec-hyp-def) along with numerical evidence
(Sec. @sec-hyps-num-evidence). Third, it was seen that
many papers claim to shine some light to the RI problem beginning, at least since
@Feelders2000RIMixtureModels, so over 25 years ago, but the literature still sees RI as
a problem where no really convincing solution has been found. I believe this comes
from the aforementioned low credibility of the results mostly because of the evaluation
methods, from the conceptional weaknesses or from the results not being widely reproducible.
Although a full answer to this shortcoming is not provided here, I give an outlook on how
to structure RI approaches using the hypotheses researched that may help alleviate the
speculated reasons from above.
